faq.a: A meander is a big loop or bend in a river, usually on flat land in its lower course. Meanders slowly move across the valley as the river erodes one bank and builds the other.

faq.q: Why does a river erode the outside of a bend?
faq.a: Water going round a bend is flung to the outside, where it flows fastest and deepest, so it wears that bank away. A spiral current also carries sand from the outside to the inside.
A floodplain is the wide, flat land beside a river that floods when the river overflows. Meanders swing across it, and floods spread fertile silt over it.
asks: Why is the land by rivers flat?

faq.a: Short straight stretches do, especially in steep mountain valleys or where people have straightened channels. But over long flat distances, rivers naturally start to bend.
A point bar is a gentle slope of sand and gravel on the inside of a river bend, where slow water drops its load.
asks: What builds up on the inside of a bend?

facts: The word meander comes from the Büyük Menderes River in Turkey, known in ancient times as the Maeander and famous for its winding course.
Meanders tend to form where rivers flow over gentle slopes with soft banks.

quiz.say: On which side of a river bend is erosion strongest?
quiz.why: The fastest water swings to the outside of the bend and wears that bank away.

wrong.1: The inside is where slow water drops sand.
wrong.2: The flow is uneven, which is why the bend grows.
